Since this loop was observed in two distinct RNA viruses, glycolysis and lactate handling may represent host-directed targets for antiviral intervention, while lactate's broader clinical relevance as an immune biomarker requires further investigation.

articles.titulo: Obesity-associated transcriptomic remodelling in hidradenitis suppurativa and treatment response.
articles.revista: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV
articles.autores: Kapur S, Solone XK, Mi R, Sidhu KS, Gershater M, Cruz J, Hamzavi I, Adrianto I, Zhou L, Mi QS
articles.resumo_original: Obesity is characterized by chronic low-grade inflammation and metabolic dysfunction. It is a major risk factor for hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), where it is associated with increased disease severity and metabolic comorbidity. Obesity promotes a pro-inflammatory, immunometabolic state marked by adipokine imbalance and alters the local skin environment through mechanical stress, occlusion and microbiome disruption. Mechanistic transcriptomic analyses further suggest that obesity induces tissue-specific changes in HS skin, including metabolic signalling in lesions and early barrier dysfunction in perilesional skin. In practice, obesity is associated with more severe and treatment-refractory disease but remains a modifiable risk factor. Weight loss, bariatric surgery and metabolism-directed therapies show potential to reduce disease burden, although controlled studies are limited. Overall, obesity acts as both a systemic and local modifier of HS, supporting its classification as an immunometabolic disorder.

articles.titulo: Anti-TNF Therapy Is Associated With Browning- and Immune-Related Changes in Creeping Fat in Crohn's Disease.
articles.autores: Monfort-Ferré D, Ginés I, Cepero C, Cabré L, Caro A, Menacho M, Gené M, Garcia M, Lahoz MDC, Mañas MJ, Martí M, Tarzán A, Suau R, Ferreres J, Manyé J, Serena C
articles.resumo_original:
Creeping fat (CrF) in Crohn's disease (CD) is a metabolically active perilesional adipose tissue involved in intestinal inflammation. Whether biological therapies modify its browning-associated phenotype remains largely unexplored. We investigated whether anti-TNF treatment is associated with changes in browning-, mitochondrial biogenesis- and immune-related pathways in CrF and whether similar molecular changes occur following ex vivo infliximab exposure.
Two independent human cohorts were analysed. (1) Observational cohort: CrF biopsies from anti-TNF-treated and anti-TNF-naïve CD patients (n = 14 and n = 19, respectively) were analysed for metabolic and inflammatory gene and protein expression. AdMSCs and mature CrF-derived adipocytes were isolated, and UCP1 protein abundance was assessed by immunohistochemistry and western blotting. (2) Ex vivo cohort: Paired CrF explants from anti-TNF-naïve patients with CD undergoing surgery were cultured with or without infliximab (5 mg/kg-equivalent, 24 h) and analysed by RT-qPCR and immunohistochemistry.
Anti-TNF-treated patients showed higher UCP1 expression in CrF at mRNA and protein levels. CrF-derived mature adipocytes from treated patients exhibited increased expression of browning-/thermogenesis- and mitochondrial biogenesis-associated genes, together with reduced selected pro-inflammatory markers. AdMSCs also showed exploratory differences in their conditioned-medium protein profile, although no protein remained significant after FDR correction. Ex vivo infliximab exposure was associated with changes in selected browning-, mitochondrial biogenesis- and immune-related markers.
Together, the observational and ex vivo findings identify CrF as an anti-TNF-responsive immunometabolic compartment in CD, characterised by coordinated browning-, mitochondrial biogenesis- and immune-related molecular changes. Functional studies are needed to establish the metabolic significance of these changes.

articles.titulo: Deciphering Host Genomic Pathway Landscapes in Severe COVID-19 by Exome Sequencing of a Large Admixed Brazilian Cohort.
articles.autores: Zetum ASS, Silva DRCD, Ventorim VDP, Mion FA, Passarela FDS, Brasil P, Campos TL, Acioli-Santos B, Oliveira FRDS, Trabach RSDR, Altoé LSC, Meira DD, Louro ID
articles.resumo_original: The host genetic factors that resulted in the heterogeneous clinical outcomes of COVID-19 remained poorly understood, especially in admixed populations that are underrepresented in global genomic studies. In this study, we investigated the genetic landscape associated with COVID-19 severity using whole-exome sequencing data from 325 Brazilian individuals recruited between 2020 and 2023. To prioritize variants related to disease severity, we applied a machine learning framework combining Support Vector Machine - Recursive Feature Elimination and SHAP interpretation. This approach encompasses 25 variants that contributed to the model's discrimination between severe and non-severe cases (AUC = 0.94) in our cohort. Subsequently, logistic regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, principal components of ancestry, and significant comorbidities confirmed several loci associated with severity after correction for multiple testing (FDR < 0.05). The prioritized genes were grouped into biological axes, including mitochondrial bioenergetics, neuroimmune signaling, complement activation, and epithelial structural integrity. Variants in genes such as MUC16, SLC4A2, LAPS1, ARRDC2, and CCSER1 showed associations with disease severity. Furthermore, functional annotation using CADD and regulatory exploration using GTEx suggested that several loci may influence gene regulation in lung, immune, and neural tissues. Instead of implicating single causal variants, our findings highlight pathway-level genetic architectures that may contribute to the variability of the host response to COVID-19. These findings provide exploratory insights into potential host genetic pathways that may be involved in disease variability in admixed environments. However, replication in independent cohorts and functional validation are still needed.

articles.titulo: Beyond the Microbial Hypothesis: Shared Genetic, Osteoimmune and Vascular Mechanisms in the Oral-Brain Axis Linking Periodontitis and Alzheimer's Disease.
articles.autores: Kabbashi S, Ahmed M, Chetty M
articles.resumo_original: Periodontitis, a chronic inflammatory disease of the tooth-supporting tissues, is increasingly linked to Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet mechanistic accounts of this 'oral-brain axis' have been dominated by microbial translocation and the gingipain hypothesis. This review argues that the convergence between periodontitis and AD extends well beyond microbes, integrating shared genetic, osteoimmune and vascular-inflammatory mechanisms that are rarely considered together. Genetic susceptibility reaches beyond APOE ε4 to the osteoprotegerin (OPG) axis, with APOE ε4 linking the two conditions through impaired amyloid-β clearance, blood-brain barrier dysfunction and altered lipid handling. The OPG/RANK/RANKL system emerges as a bone-brain (osteoimmune) interface, in which OPG shows a dual-role paradox, reduced locally in periodontal bone loss yet elevated systematically in AD, while soluble RANKL displays neuroprotective properties. Because OPG acts as a decoy receptor for RANKL, we hypothesise that elevated OPG in AD limits RANKL-dependent microglial amyloid-β clearance. Endothelial dysfunction, reflected in circulating endocan, provides a shared vascular readout that is raised in both diseases and responsive to periodontal therapy. We propose that these genetic, microbial and vascular inputs converge on microglial priming and trained immunity, a unifying immunological node through which chronic peripheral inflammation may act during the decades-long preclinical phase of AD. Current evidence nonetheless remains predominantly associative, causality is unproven and mechanistic data rely heavily on animal models. The oral-brain axis is therefore best regarded as a promising yet still unproven framework in which osteoimmune and vascular pathways, and candidate biomarkers such as endocan, represent underexplored targets for future longitudinal and interventional research.

articles.titulo: Single-Cell Characterization of SPP1-Expressing Macrophages and Their Predicted Interactions With T Cells in the Breast Cancer Bone Metastatic Microenvironment.
articles.autores: Xuan Z, Wu Z, Zhong Y, Jiang J, Zhang Y, Cheng L, Zhang J, Wang K
articles.resumo_original:
Breast cancer is a highly common malignancy in women, with bone as its most frequent site of distant metastasis significantly increasing mortality risk.
This study integrated single-cell RNA sequencing datasets (GSE266330 and GSE243526) to systematically characterize the tumor microenvironment across normal tissue, primary tumor, and bone metastasis in breast cancer.
In total, 141 056 high-quality single cells were analyzed from an integrated cohort comprising a bone-metastasis dataset (GSE266330) and a primary/normal breast dataset (GSE243526), identifying 11 major cell types. Within the bone-metastatic cohort, we identified a macrophage subpopulation highly expressing SPP1 (Mac-SPP1) that exhibited an M2-polarized signature and elevated metabolic gene-set enrichment, and that expressed transcription factors such as HOXA9 and MAF. We also identified CD4-S100A9 and CD8-GZMK T-cell subpopulations with high cytotoxicity, high exhaustion, and metabolic reprogramming. Pseudotime analysis positioned CD4-S100A9 cells at one end of the inferred CD4+ T-cell trajectory and CD8-GZMK cells at an intermediate node along the inferred CD8+ T-cell trajectory. Cell-cell communication analysis predicted that Mac-SPP1 interacts with these T-cell subsets through the SPP1-integrin (e.g., SPP1-CD44) and CD74-MIF/COPA signaling axes.
This study provides a single-cell characterization of the breast cancer bone-metastatic microenvironment, identifying an SPP1-expressing macrophage subset (Mac-SPP1) and predicting its interactions with CD4-S100A9 and CD8-GZMK T cells. Because the bone-metastatic and primary/normal specimens derive from different datasets, these findings are descriptive and cannot be attributed to metastatic progression alone and require experimental validation and confirmation in cohorts that profile primary and metastatic specimens within a single study.

articles.titulo: Interleukin-37 in cancer: Context-dependent roles in tumor immunity, prognosis, and therapeutic targeting.
articles.revista: The Journal of international medical research
articles.autores: Zhang Y, Wang X, Xu M, Zhang T
articles.resumo_original: Interleukin-37, a member of the interleukin-1 family, is increasingly recognized as a regulator of cancer biology and tumor immunity. Across cancer types, interleukin-37 expression exhibits divergent patterns and clinical associations. In non-small cell lung cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, colorectal cancer, renal cell carcinoma, and acute myeloid leukemia, decreased interleukin-37 expression is more often associated with aggressive clinicopathologic features and poor outcomes. By contrast, in gastric cancer, epithelial ovarian cancer, melanoma, and several other malignancies, increased interleukin-37 expression has been linked to tumor progression and adverse prognosis. Mechanistically, interleukin-37 acts through intracellular and extracellular pathways, including Smad3-dependent nuclear translocation and signaling through the interleukin-18 receptor alpha/interleukin-1 receptor 8 complex, with downstream effects on signal transducer and activator of transcription 3, nuclear factor kappa B, transforming growth factor beta/Smad, and related networks. Depending on cancer type, immune context, isoform usage, and disease stage, interleukin-37 may inhibit proliferation, metabolic reprogramming, angiogenesis, invasion, and metastatic dissemination or promote immune suppression and premetastatic niche formation. Beyond its tumor-intrinsic effects, interleukin-37 reshapes the tumor microenvironment by modulating macrophages, dendritic cells, natural killer cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and T-cell subsets. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on the dual roles of interleukin-37 in cancer, discusses major sources of inconsistency across studies, and highlights its potential relevance to prognostic stratification, biomarker development, and therapeutic targeting.

articles.titulo: Cellular metabolic reprogramming in periodontitis: advanced therapeutic strategies and periodontal regeneration.
articles.autores: Sun C, Wei J, Liu M, Tang D, Tan B, Li H, Chen Z, Ou Q
articles.resumo_original:
Periodontitis is one of the most prevalent chronic inflammatory diseases worldwide, ultimately leading to tooth loss and masticatory dysfunction. Effective treatment of periodontitis requires not only control of inflammation but also regeneration of various cell types and tissues. Recent studies have shown that metabolic reprogramming in the periodontal microenvironment serves as a key link between inflammatory responses and an imbalance in bone homeostasis. Metabolic reprogramming not only drives disease progression but also profoundly influences tissue repair.
of review: This article provides a comprehensive review of metabolic reprogramming in immune cells and bone-related cells during periodontitis, with a particular focus on how metabolic abnormalities impair the osteogenic differentiation capacity of periodontal ligament stem cells and disrupt the balance between osteogenesis and osteolysis. Additionally, we highlight therapeutic strategies targeting metabolic pathways, especially those based on biomaterials, which can modulate the metabolism of immune cells and bone cells for periodontal regeneration. Finally, this review discusses future directions and emerging technologies in this field, aiming to offer theoretical support and clinical reference for a deeper understanding ofthe intricate interactive network of cell metabolism, immune response and bone remodeling and to develop precise strategies for periodontitis. Key scientific concepts of review: During periodontitis, distinct cell populations exhibit unique metabolic phenotypes: immune cells sustain inflammation via glycolysis, while bone-resident cells undergo metabolic shifts that impair their regenerative capacity. Restoring metabolic balance suppresses aberrant immunity, enhances bone formation, and creates a favorable microenvironment for periodontal regeneration. This review highlights emerging therapeutic strategies targeting metabolic pathways, particularly metabolism-modulating biomaterials. By integrating current advances, this review aims to elucidate the links among metabolism, immunity, and bone homeostasis, offering new directions for precise regenerative therapies in periodontitis.

articles.titulo: A tumor-microenvironment-responsive M1 macrophage-membrane-camouflaged nanoplatform potentiates polyphyllin VII immunotherapy through disrupting the ASNS-mTOR axis and inducing immunogenic cell death for solid tumor treatment.
articles.autores: Su W, Tian L, Xu H, Wang J, Li X, Gao W
articles.resumo_original: Polyphyllin VII, a steroidal saponin derived from Paris polyphylla, exhibits potent anti-tumor activity across multiple cancer types. Its clinical application is severely hampered by poor water solubility, non-specific biodistribution, and inherent cytotoxicity to normal tissues. Here, we report a rationally engineered biomimetic nanoplatform -M1-PVII·MSN@PDA- that systematically addresses these translational bottlenecks through a tri-functional design: mesoporous silica nanoparticles (MSNs) provide high-capacity drug loading and aqueous dispersibility; a polydopamine (PDA) coating serves as a tumor-microenvironment-responsive molecular gatekeeper, preventing premature drug leakage during systemic circulation while enabling pH/ near-infrared (NIR)-triggered release at tumor sites; and M1 macrophage membrane camouflage confers immune evasion, prolonged circulation, and active tumor homing through inherited surface proteins including CD47 and integrin α4/β1. Comprehensive in vitro and in vivo characterization demonstrates that this nanoparticle achieves a high PVII loading efficiency, suppresses premature drug release in physiological conditions, and selectively releases its payload under tumor-mimicking acidic and oxidative conditions. Mechanistically, released PVII disrupts the asparagine synthetase (ASNS)-mTOR signaling axis, inducing metabolic reprogramming and asparagine depletion in tumor cells, thereby suppressing proliferation and triggering immunogenic cell death (ICD) characterized by calreticulin (CRT) exposure and HMGB1 release. ICD-driven danger signals promote dendritic cell (DC) maturation, facilitate cytotoxic T-lymphocyte infiltration, and reshape the immunosuppressive TME toward an immunostimulatory phenotype. In murine solid tumor models, M1-PVII·MSN@PDA demonstrates superior tumor suppression, enhanced immune activation, and favorable biosafety profiles compared to free PVII. Collectively, this work establishes a mechanistically grounded, multi-functional nanoimmunotherapy strategy that integrates metabolic intervention with innate immune reprogramming, providing a translational framework for next-generation solid tumor treatment.

articles.titulo: Comparative Effects of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists and DPP-4 Inhibitors on Sepsis in Patients with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: A Population-Based Cohort Study.
articles.revista: International journal of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
articles.autores: Wu TJ, Chen CH, Wu HC, Wang YH, Wang CY, Lai CC
articles.resumo_original:
Sepsis is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Antihyperglycemic agents may influence infection risk through distinct immunometabolic pathways. We compared glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) with dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (DPP-4is) in patients with COPD and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).
This population-based, active-comparator, new-user cohort study used the TriNetX Global Network. Adults aged 40-100 years with COPD and T2DM who initiated a GLP-1RA or DPP-4i between 2007 and 2019 were included. Propensity score matching (1:1) adjusted for demographics, BMI, HbA1c, COPD severity proxies, comorbidities, and medications. The primary outcome was sepsis; secondary outcomes were pneumonia, severe sepsis, and all-cause mortality, assessed at 1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 months.
Before matching, 21,622 patients started a GLP-1RA and 67,259 a DPP-4i; after matching, 20,074 remained in each group with balanced characteristics (all standardized mean differences <0.10). Compared with DPP-4i users, GLP-1RA users had a significantly lower risk of sepsis at 1 year (hazard ratio [HR] 0.852; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.770-0.942). The risks of secondary outcomes at 1 year were numerically lower in the GLP-1RA group, with statistically significant reductions in pneumonia (HR 0.729; 95% CI 0.671-0.792) and all-cause mortality (HR 0.656; 95% CI 0.587-0.732), while the association with severe sepsis did not reach statistical significance (HR 0.891; 95% CI 0.770-1.033).
In patients with COPD and T2DM, initiation of GLP-1RAs was associated with lower risks of sepsis, pneumonia, and all-cause mortality compared with DPP-4is. However, given the observational design, causality cannot be established and residual confounding remains a potential limitation. While these findings suggest potential benefits of GLP-1RAs beyond glycemic control, further confirmation through randomized controlled trials is warranted to guide clinical decision-making.

articles.titulo: Metabolic reprogramming in macrophages: the central role of lipid metabolism in bone homeostasis.
articles.autores: Li L, Zhang Y, Huang S, Xiao Y, Liu G, Wu Z, Hu Y, Gong S, Mao J, Song K, Li Q
articles.resumo_original: Macrophage lipid metabolism is a pivotal regulator of bone homeostasis. Macrophages orchestrate the balance between bone resorption and formation primarily through their M1/M2 polarization states, with M1 macrophages promoting resorption and M2 macrophages supporting formation. This review comprehensively describes how key lipid metabolic pathways, such as fatty acid oxidation (FAO) and cholesterol metabolism, govern this polarization and subsequent bone remodeling. It integrates the core mechanisms by which lipid metabolism drives M1 and M2 polarization, and highlights that targeting macrophage lipid metabolism represents a promising therapeutic strategy for bone diseases. Finally, we identify emerging frontiers, including the "gut-bone axis" and epigenetic regulation, as critical directions for future research.

articles.titulo: Cross-kingdom endosymbiosis rewires the rhizobiome for fungal pathogenicity.
articles.autores: Fu W, Sun C, Guo Q, Lai H
articles.resumo_original: Soil-borne fungal pathogens undermine crop health by disrupting the protective rhizosphere microbiome. Zhou et al. uncovered a cross-kingdom endosymbiotic mechanism that enables Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici to subvert rhizosphere protection: intracellular bacterial endosymbionts drive fungal metabolic reprogramming to produce a selective toxin, thereby suppressing keystone beneficial rhizobacteria.

articles.titulo: Loss of T cell-intrinsic Keap1 alleviates colitis by suppressing Th17 differentiation and enhancing regulatory T cell functions.
articles.autores: Dasgupta D, Tripathi A, Griffard-Smith R, Dahabieh MS, Saif MSI, Roy BC, Burt E, Ellis A, Sheldon RD, Dhorajiya P, Umar S, Koestler D, Jones RG, Pyaram K
articles.resumo_original: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a form of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) characterized by chronic inflammation in the colon. In this study, we elucidate the roles of antioxidation proteins Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1) and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) in modulating CD4+ T cell differentiation and intestinal inflammation in UC. Using mice with T cell-specific deletion of Keap1 or Nrf2, we demonstrate that T cell-intrinsic Nrf2 levels influence T helper (Th) cell differentiation, intestinal inflammation and colitis disease outcome. Loss of Keap1 in T cells suppressed proinflammatory Th1 and Th17 subset differentiation, while promoting induced regulatory T-cell (iTreg) generation in an Nrf2-dependent manner, thereby alleviating intestinal inflammation and protecting against colitis. Mechanistic analyses revealed that Keap1 deletion was associated with metabolic reprogramming in iTregs, characterized by increased glutamine utilization and enhanced mitochondrial respiration, suggesting that these metabolic changes may contribute to enhanced iTreg generation. Further, analyses of UC patient tissues and omics datasets revealed increased Nrf2 gene expression and enrichment of Nrf2-associated transcriptional signatures in colonic Tregs, correlating with Foxp3 expression. In summary, our findings identify Keap1-Nrf2 axis as an important regulator of iTreg generation and function, suggesting that targeting this pathway may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for IBD.

articles.titulo: Psychobiotic modulation of the microbiome-gut-brain axis: A systematic review of the literature.
articles.autores: Rendeiro J, Santos VH, Silva-Vaz P
articles.resumo_original:
Major depressive disorder (MDD) is incompletely explained by the monoaminergic model. The microbiome-gut-brain (MGB) axis may link gut microbial ecology to immune, metabolic, neuroendocrine and neural signalling relevant to mood and antidepressant response.
To synthesise recent evidence on (I) microbiota-targeted (psychobiotic) interventions; (II) the gut microbiome as a diagnostic and treatment-response biomarker; and (III) biopsychosocial and immunometabolic correlates of depression.
PubMed, Scopus and PubPsych were searched (January 2022 to February 2025) following PRISMA 2020. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2, ROBINS-I and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Findings were synthesised narratively, stratified by population, intervention type and study design.
Sixty-six studies were included: 36 in diagnosed depressive disorders, 10 in non-clinical samples, 15 in other medical conditions and 5 genetic or biobank analyses; most were of low or very low methodological quality. Depression was associated with lower abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa and with altered tryptophan, bile acid, inflammatory and barrier-related markers, largely in cross-sectional designs. In MDD, some strain-specific add-on probiotics were associated with greater symptom reduction than placebo, whereas others showed no benefit; prebiotic, dietary and faecal microbiota transplantation data were sparse or derived from non-MDD populations. Diagnostic and treatment-response models came from small samples and were rarely externally validated.
The gut microbiome is a plausible contributor to depressive pathophysiology and treatment variability, but current evidence is heterogeneous, predominantly associative and of low certainty. Psychobiotic interventions and microbiome-based biomarkers remain investigational; adequately powered, strain- and dose-specific trials and independently validated models are required before clinical application.

articles.titulo: UBE2T-driven lipid metabolic reprogramming links chronic inflammation to pancreatic cancer progression.
articles.revista: Pancreatology : official journal of the International Association of Pancreatology (IAP) ... [et al.]
articles.autores: Xiao L, Ma Y, Li J, Cai W, Long B, Zhou H, Jiao Z
articles.resumo_original:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly lethal malignancy closely associated with chronic inflammation. However, the molecular link between persistent inflammatory signaling and lipid metabolic reprogramming during PDAC progression remains incompletely understood. We investigated the role of ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme E2T (UBE2T) in this process.
The effects of UBE2T were evaluated using cellular functional assays, lipidomic profiling, pathway-rescue experiments, and genetically engineered mouse models under chronic inflammatory conditions. The therapeutic effects of β-1,2,3,4,6-pentagalloylglucose (PGG), previously identified as a pharmacological inhibitor of UBE2T, were further assessed in vitro and in vivo.
Inflammatory stimulation increased UBE2T expression, whereas UBE2T depletion suppressed PDAC cell proliferation and motility- and invasion-associated phenotypes. Lipidomic analyses revealed extensive UBE2T-dependent remodeling of pancreatic lipid profiles and reduced lipid accumulation following UBE2T loss. UBE2T depletion decreased AKT phosphorylation, sterol regulatory element-binding protein (SREBP1) nuclear accumulation, and fatty acid synthase (FASN) expression. AKT activation partially rescued these alterations, whereas SREBP1 knockdown or AKT inhibition attenuated UBE2T-induced TG accumulation, supporting the involvement of the AKT/SREBP1/FASN axis. In vivo, UBE2T deficiency alleviated inflammation-associated pancreatic pathological progression and reduced pancreatic lipid accumulation. PGG treatment similarly reduced lesion burden, FASN expression, and pancreatic lipid accumulation, with concomitant attenuation of stromal remodeling.
UBE2T links chronic inflammatory signaling to AKT/SREBP1/FASN-associated lipid metabolic reprogramming during PDAC progression. UBE2T deficiency and PGG treatment attenuated pancreatic pathological progression and lipid metabolic remodeling, supporting UBE2T as a potential therapeutic target for PDAC.

articles.titulo: IL-33 modulates maternal-fetal macrophage immunometabolism and is associated with attenuation of MIA-associated behavioral abnormalities in adult offspring.
articles.autores: Zhu X, Shen C, He K, Chang H, Qiu J, Chen L, Chen L, Hou M, Ji M, Xu Z
articles.resumo_original: Maternal immune activation (MIA) is a pivotal risk factor for neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism spectrum disorder. However, the mechanisms of MIA at the maternal-fetal interface remain elusive. Here, we used soluble tachyzoite antigen (STAg) from Toxoplasma gondii to induce MIA in pregnant mice at E14.5, followed by maternal administration of interleukin-33 (IL-33) from E15.5 to E17.5. Proteomic profiling coupled with protein-protein interaction network analysis nominated IL-33 as a candidate immunoregulatory factor. In exploratory analyses, maternal IL-33 administration was associated with shifts in macrophage-associated immune profiles, reduced placental inflammation, and attenuated MIA-associated behavioral abnormalities in adult offspring. Given that suppression of tumorigenicity 2 (ST2) is the cognate receptor for IL-33, we next interrogated this pathway in ST2-deficient mice. ST2 deficiency abolished the effects of IL-33 on macrophage repolarization and inflammatory homeostasis, and the behavioral improvements were not evident in ST2-deficient offspring. Mechanistically, IL-33 administration was associated with reduced glycolytic features and improved mitochondrial function in macrophages, consistent with partial restoration of immunometabolic homeostasis at the maternal-fetal interface. Collectively, our findings highlight an immunometabolic axis in STAg-induced MIA pathogenesis, revealing IL-33/ST2 signaling as a potential experimental target for mitigating MIA-associated immune and behavioral abnormalities.

articles.titulo: Pathophysiology-guided nutritional strategies for persistent inflammation, immunosuppression, and catabolism syndrome: an immunometabolic perspective.
articles.autores: Wu Z, Yao B
articles.resumo_original: Persistent inflammation, immunosuppression, and catabolism syndrome (PICS) is a phenotype of chronic critical illness characterized by unresolved inflammation, impaired immune competence, sustained catabolism, skeletal muscle loss, recurrent infections, and poor functional recovery. Although guideline-based nutritional support remains fundamental, persistent immunometabolic abnormalities may limit responsiveness to nutrient delivery and contribute to anabolic resistance, impaired substrate utilization, and defective tissue repair. This mini-review examines biological mechanisms limiting nutritional responsiveness in PICS and evaluates evidence for pathophysiology-guided nutritional strategies. A structured literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science was conducted from database inception through September 6, 2026, prioritizing English-language clinical guidelines, clinical studies, and mechanistic or translational evidence relevant to PICS, critical illness, nutritional responsiveness, and immunometabolic nutrition. We propose a framework addressing major barriers to recovery through strategies to restore anabolic responsiveness with protein, leucine, and rehabilitation; modulate inflammatory resolution and immune dysfunction with omega-3 fatty acids and arginine; optimize nutrient timing and circadian-metabolic regulation; and maintain a metabolic milieu conducive to nutrient utilization. Because direct interventional evidence in well-defined PICS populations remains limited, these strategies should complement rather than replace guideline-based nutritional support. The framework is conceptual and hypothesis-generating, and prospective PICS-specific studies incorporating biological stratification and clinically meaningful recovery outcomes are needed to determine its translational value.

articles.titulo: Mitochondrial quality-control uncoupling in sepsis: a missing link to persistent immune hyporesponsiveness.
articles.autores: Zhang Y, Xia XP, Zhao L
articles.resumo_original: Sepsis imposes competing demands for antimicrobial activity and organelle maintenance. Mitochondrial recovery requires coordinated damage containment, selective removal, lysosomal degradation and recycling, and functional replacement. We define mitochondrial quality-control uncoupling as a mismatch among these processes. When damage outpaces completed clearance, dysfunctional mitochondria retain redox and danger-signaling activity. When removal outpaces replacement, mitochondrial mass and spare respiratory capacity decline. Incomplete lysosomal processing can combine both phenotypes by removing mitochondria from the functional network while retaining undegraded cargo. Immune cells may therefore remain viable yet fail to increase metabolic and biosynthetic output during renewed challenge. Inhibitory immune signaling can further restrict substrate use and mitochondrial rebuilding, reinforcing mitochondrial and immune dysfunction. This framework reconciles divergent observations on mitophagy and explains how inflammation can coexist with ineffective host defense. We define state-matched longitudinal phenotyping as repeated, cell-type-specific assessment of damage burden, clearance completion, respiratory reserve and immune function over time. Such phenotyping could guide interventions toward the dominant defect rather than indiscriminately activating a single pathway.

articles.titulo: Nanomedicine and the innate immune system: immunogenicity, nanoparticle-immune cell interactions and implications for cancer immunotherapy.
articles.autores: Bozzuto G, Stringaro A, Migani S, Colone M, Calcabrini A, Dupuis ML
articles.resumo_original: Nanoparticles were initially considered inert carriers for therapeutic payloads. This view has evolved substantially, as a growing body of experimental and clinical evidence indicates that engineered nanoparticles act as active immunomodulators, engaging pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), activating the complement cascade, reprogramming macrophage polarization, and inducing trained immunity in innate immune cells. This dual role of nanoparticles as both immunological agents and delivery vehicles represents a fundamental change that demands an integrative framework combining immunogenicity assessment, nanotoxicology, and therapeutic exploitation. This review provides an overview of the current state of the art at the nanomedicine-innate immunity interface across six nanoparticle classes, adopting a comparative framework that identifies both the immunological mechanisms shared among platforms and the specific features that distinguish individual nanoparticle systems. The analysis focuses on key innate immune populations, including dendritic cells (DCs), macrophages, natural killer (NK) cells, neutrophils and mast cells, as well as major innate immune signaling pathways, including the cyclic guanosine monophosphate-adenosine monophosphate synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway, Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling, and the NOD-like receptor protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome. The innate immune system represents a primary determinant of the biological outcome of nanomaterial exposure and provides a critical link to subsequent adaptive responses. Two methodological themes recur throughout the analysis. The first concerns attribution: distinguishing responses driven by the carrier itself from those driven by its cargo or by contaminants requires defined controls, and in their absence an observed response should not be ascribed to the nanomaterial. The second is inter-individual variability, which emerges as a determinant of outcome rather than as experimental noise, and which appears to arise from the combination of recipient and platform rather than from either alone, so that susceptibility established for one platform does not transfer to another. Our aim is to highlight unexplored connections and experimental gaps that currently limit clinical translation, offering an integrated interpretation of nanoparticle-innate immunity interactions that points to unresolved immunological challenges and oncology-relevant therapeutic opportunities for each class still awaiting validation.

articles.titulo: Beyond the classical Fc receptor: CD64 in phagocytosis and trained immunity.
articles.autores: Qu Z, Zhang H, Shapiro SD, Xiao G
articles.resumo_original: CD64 (FcγRI) is traditionally categorized as the high-affinity receptor for immunoglobulin G (IgG) and as a downstream effector of adaptive humoral responses for myeloid-driven clearance and immune programs. Accumulating evidence in myeloid cell biology, however, highlights a major historical oversight: CD64 also operates as a multimodal innate immunoreceptor capable of antibody-independent pattern recognition receptor (PRR) behavior. Synthesizing over three decades of data, this review spotlights the direct interaction of CD64 with humoral pentraxins and microbial outer membrane structures independent of IgG opsonization. We consolidate the biological mechanisms by which CD64 functions as an opsonin receptor or a direct PRR to drive phagocytosis and immune signaling pathways. Because trained immunity is antibody-independent, we introduce an unaddressed paradigm for how CD64 utilizes its non-classical, primordial PRR identity to guide myeloid cells to establish and maintain innate immune memory. This framework resolves a profound evolutionary and teleological conundrum: why frontline myeloid lineages constitutively express and exponentially upregulate CD64 days before pathogen-specific antibodies are manufactured, leveraging an ancient, non-specific pattern-sensing scaffold. Finally, we conceptualize the multi-tiered regulation of CD64 as a precise, localized translational target and predictive biomarker to safely bypass the potential risks of global metabolic and epigenetic therapies.

articles.titulo: Macrophages as orchestrators of gut-organ axis crosstalk: immunometabolic reprogramming and host-directed therapy in sepsis.
articles.revista: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
articles.autores: Zeng W, Zhang Y, Fan L, Xun Y, Jiang Z, Dai F
articles.resumo_original: Sepsis is a life-threatening syndrome driven by a dysregulated host response to infection. Among the numerous contributory factors, the gut microbiota and its metabolites are increasingly recognized as potential modulators of systemic inflammation, acting through multiple gut-organ axes. Within this network, macrophages serve as central integrators that transduce microbial signals into organ-specific inflammatory or reparative outcomes. Disease evolution is critically determined by immune-metabolic reprogramming of macrophages. This reprogramming comprises tricarboxylic acid cycle truncation, lipid remodeling, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammasome activation. These processes are closely intertwined with NFκB, cGAS-STING, TLR/MyD88, and aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling. Gut-derived metabolites, particularly short-chain fatty acids and indole derivatives, shape macrophage functions in distal organs. These mechanisms predominantly operate during the acute phase of sepsis, driving early organ injury. In contrast, sepsis survivors often enter a distinct chronic phase, characterized by persistent immune dysregulation. Trained immunity, through metabolic-epigenetic rewiring, may underlie this long-term dysfunction in survivors. Preclinical promise has been demonstrated by host-directed therapies that target macrophage metabolism. Nevertheless, major challenges impede clinical translation. These include inadequate preclinical models, the absence of validated real-time biomarkers for immune-metabolic phenotyping, and marked heterogeneity among patients. This review positions macrophages as actionable sentinels in gut-organ crosstalk during acute sepsis, and further explores their role in chronic sequelae, underscoring the need for biomarker-guided stratification and precision immune-metabolic editing to overcome barriers in both settings.

articles.titulo: Blocks, Pins, and Heavy Metal: Optimized Sample Preparation for Volume EM of Myelin in Mouse Central Nervous System.
articles.autores: Ruhwedel T, Wrede C, Hegermann J, Steyer AM, Möbius W
articles.resumo_original: Volume electron microscopy is a widely used technique to image complex tissue architecture at high resolution for 3D reconstruction. Originally developed for brain connectomics, this technology has proven important for other applications as well. Here we describe protocols established in our laboratories for the visualization of myelin in the mouse central nervous system. The main purpose of the protocol is the optimized preparation of small samples such as vibratome slices or optic nerves. We include possible substitutions for toxic chemicals in commonly used protocols. Tannic acid and neodymium acetate turned out suitable for the replacement of thiocarbohydrazide and uranyl acetate.

articles.titulo: Mass Spectrometry-Based Footprinting Strategies for GPCR Structure Analysis.
articles.revista: Journal of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry
articles.autores: Jin YT, Roberts R, Smith CG, Sun J
articles.resumo_original: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are a major class of membrane proteins that mediate diverse signaling pathways and represent the largest family of drug targets. However, their conformational flexibility and structural sensitivity to membrane environments make it difficult to characterize using conventional structural methods such as X-ray crystallography, cryo-electron microscopy, and NMR. Mass spectrometry (MS)-based footprinting has been a powerful approach for probing GPCR structure and dynamics. Well-designed footprinting strategies report on solvent accessibility changes with distinct spatial and temporal resolutions. In this review, we discuss how temporal footprinting and native-like membrane mimetics such as liposomes, nanodiscs, picodiscs, and styrene maleic acid lipid particles (SMALPs) have expanded the ability to characterize GPCR dynamics under relevant physiological conditions. We also focus on four representative footprinting techniques, including fast photochemical oxidation of proteins (FPOP), synchrotron X-ray footprinting, carbene labeling, and hydrogen-deuterium exchange (HDX), and discuss the structural information on GPCRs that each method provides. We highlight the differences of each approach when analyzing GPCRs, including labeling chemistry, time scale, residue specificity, and structural resolution. We also summarize their applications in studying GPCR/ligand interaction and conformational transitions. Finally, we discuss current challenges and future opportunities for integrating footprinting techniques to achieve a more comprehensive understanding of the GPCR structure relevant to drug discovery.

articles.titulo: Brain-wide activity imaging with electron microscopy reveals a distributed brain network for processing threatening somatosensory stimuli.
articles.autores: Randel N, Wang C, Clayton MS, Wang K, Pang S, Xu CS, Champion AS, Hess HF, Cardona A, Keller PJ, Zlatic M
articles.resumo_original: To understand how brains work, neural activity must be overlayed onto synaptic-resolution circuit architecture. Recent advances in light-sheet microscopy (LSM) enable whole-brain, cellular-resolution imaging of activity of all cell bodies; however, most neurons from such datasets cannot be identified. In most organisms, neurons are identifiable based on their projections (and not based on cell body position), which, when densely labeled, cannot be resolved using LSM. Here, we present a novel methodology to overcome this by combining whole-brain activity imaging with subsequent volume electron microscopy imaging of the same brain to visualize neuronal projections and identify neurons with interesting activity. We used this approach to identify brain neurons that process input from multisensory (nociceptive and mechanosensory) Basin interneurons that trigger vigorous escape in Drosophila larvae in response to threatening somatosensory stimuli. After whole-brain imaging of neuronal activity during Basin activation, we imaged the same brain with an enhanced focused ion-beam electron microscope (eFIB-SEM). We registered the functional and anatomical volumes and reconstructed (in the eFIB-SEM volume) the projections of neurons that responded to Basin activation to determine their developmental lineage and identity. This revealed a distributed network for processing threatening somatosensory stimuli that trigger vigorous escape spanning 25 distinct lineages and many distinct brain areas. Our workflow provides a powerful framework for mapping neuronal activity onto structure across an entire brain, yielding novel insights into the distributed central processing of somatosensory stimuli.

articles.titulo: Stacking Up: The Expanding Catalog of Filament-Forming Enzymes.
articles.autores: Horton NC
articles.resumo_original: Enzyme filamentation has emerged as a widespread and functionally important mode of macromolecular organization. Once viewed as an unusual property of a few metabolic enzymes, reversible filament formation is now known for more than 50 enzymes across bacteria, archaea, plants, fungi, and animals. This review summarizes recent progress in the field, expanding substantially on our 2019 analysis and incorporating more than 300 new publications. We survey the known filament-forming enzymes, their catalytic activities, biological contexts, filament architectures, and available structural information from X-ray crystallography, cryo-electron microscopy, and in cellulo imaging approaches. Filamenting enzymes span five major enzyme classes and function in metabolism, stress responses, signaling, replication, and host defense. In many cases, polymerization occurs at critical metabolic branch points and appears to regulate enzyme activity, allostery, substrate channeling, localization, or sequestration. Distinct filament geometries, including linear stacks, solenoidal coils, tubes, and rings, are associated with specific functional outcomes and cellular roles. We also highlight emerging in cellulo structural studies of enzyme filaments, summarizing the insights they provide into filament organization and cellular assembly when available. Together, these findings highlight enzyme filamentation as a common mode of macromolecular organization with consequences for structure, assembly, and function in diverse biological contexts.

articles.titulo: Cryo-EM and NMR Reveal a Membrane-Gated Doc2B-Munc13-1 Complex and a Helical Doc2B-SNARE-Binding Interface.
articles.autores: Rastegar CT, Powell J, Wosztyl A, David G, Jaczynska K, Bai XC, Han Y, Chen Z, Rizo J
articles.resumo_original: Doc2s modulate neurotransmitter release through interactions with Munc13-1, SNAREs, lipids, and Ca2+, which involve the Doc2 C2 domains and Munc13-interacting domain (MID). However, it is unclear how these interactions are coupled, how Doc2s bind to Munc13-1, and how they bind to the SNAREs. Here we determined the cryo-electron microscopy structure of a Doc2B-Munc13-1 complex aided by an AI-designed Munc13-1 binder, revealing how Doc2B MID binds to a Munc13-1 hydrophobic pocket essential for opening syntaxin-1 and explaining why Doc2B inhibits SNARE assembly. NMR and fluorescence spectroscopy show that Doc2B MID binds lipids and that MID-lipid and MID-Munc13-1 interactions are mutually exclusive, suggesting that membrane binding helps release the inhibition of Munc13-1. NMR shows that Doc2B binds to the SNARE complex via two helices of C2B. Based on these results and liposome fusion assays, we propose a working model whereby: 1. Doc2B MID-Munc13-1 interactions facilitate synergistic binding of both proteins to the plasma membrane, with the MID inhibiting Munc13-1. 2. Membrane binding facilitates MID-lipid interactions that transiently relieve the inhibition of Munc13-1, allowing SNARE complex assembly. 3. Doc2B binding to the SNARE complex inhibits neurotransmitter release but generates a primed state that mediates neurotransmitter release by an as-yet-unknown mechanism.

articles.titulo: Axon Content of the Circumpapillary Nerve Fiber Layer in Experimental Glaucoma.
articles.autores: Kharal A, Sullivan M, Patel NB
articles.resumo_original:
To determine axonal content from optical coherence tomography (OCT)-derived circumpapillary retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) measures using histologically informed models in a non-human primate experimental glaucoma model.
Unilateral experimental glaucoma was induced in 22 animals (mean age, 6.1 ± 1.9 years; 10 females) who were monitored with OCT. At varying stages of neuropathy, animals were euthanized and perfusion fixed. For RNFL histology, circumpapillary tissue (∼0.75 × 0.75 mm) from six equally spaced regions was obtained and processed for serial block face scanning electron microscopy in five animals. A single high-resolution image of the block face was used to quantify axon size (cross-sectional area) and non-axonal tissue area within the RNFL. Using the 95% limits of the histological data as a starting point, models for estimating axon count from OCT RNFL area were optimized and compared to total retrobulbar optic nerve axon counts in 22 animals.
The mean circumpapillary RNFL thickness of control eyes was 112 ± 6 µm, and it was 70 ± 24 µm in eyes with experimental glaucoma. Axon size and non-axonal area varied across the circumpapillary regions (F5, 31 = 9.06 and F5, 36 = 3.94, respectively; both P < 0.01), but did not differ between the two eyes (F1, 22 = 0.59, P = 0.45 and F1, 15 = 2.10, P = 0.17). The optimized model for estimating axon content from the circumpapillary RNFL profile had good agreement with the retrobulbar axon count (mean difference = 25; 95% limits of agreement, -334,239 to 334,289).
The axon size distribution and non-axonal area in the circumpapillary RNFL are similar between healthy and stable glaucomatous eyes. Building on this, a location-specific model is proposed that estimates axon content from the circumpapillary RNFL profile after accounting for regional variability in axonal and non-axonal components.

articles.titulo: 3D Electron Diffraction Reveals Counterion Coordination in Co-Existing Polymorphs of Ag29 Nanocluster.
articles.autores: Nagar H, Gurung K, Kučeráková M, Som A, Palatinus L, Pradeep T
articles.resumo_original: We unravel the complete structural architecture of the polymorphic Na3[Ag29(BDT)12(TPP)4] nanocluster (NC) using three-dimensional electron diffraction (3D ED) of microscopic crystals. By drop-casting nanocluster solution directly onto microscopy grids, we achieve in situ crystallization of nanometer-sized polymorphs and independently resolve co-existing cubic and trigonal phases crystal-by-crystal from a single grid square. Using difference electrostatic potential (DESP) maps derived from empirical 3D ED data, we pinpoint the specific lattice locations of the elusive Na+ counterions and observe distinct coordination environments across the two polymorphs. In the densely packed, solvent-free cubic phase, Na+ binds exclusively to thermodynamically favored pockets formed by one core-anchored and two staple sulfur atoms. Conversely, within the open, solvated trigonal lattice, Na+ occupies both these core-anchored sites and alternative positions coordinated entirely by three sulfur atoms of an outer Ag3S3 staple motif. These findings establish 3D ED as a powerful tool for resolving nanoscale polymorphic mixtures and demonstrate how macroscopic crystal packing influences local ionic interactions, providing key structural insights for the design of cluster-based assemblies.

articles.titulo: An evaluation framework for sparse 4D (3D + time) imaging reconstruction via bootstrapped cross-validation.
articles.autores: Zhang Y, Yao Z, Hu Z, Ritschel T, Villanueva-Perez P
articles.resumo_original: Four-dimensional (4D; 3D + time) microscopic imaging has emerged as a powerful technique for investigating dynamic phenomena in complex systems, enabling direct visualisation of structural evolution in space and time. However, when pushing the limits of spatiotemporal resolution, most time-resolved imaging techniques yield inherently sparse 4D datasets. While deep learning-based reconstruction methods have shown promise in reconstructing 4D from sparse spatiotemporal measurements, a practical approach for evaluating their performance in the absence of a 4D reference has, to the best of our knowledge, been lacking. Here, we present a bootstrapped cross-validation framework that estimates reconstruction performance by quantifying correlations between reconstructions generated from independently sampled subsets of the acquired data, as inspired by the 3D validation strategy in cryo-electron microscopy, where reconstructions from split datasets are compared to assess resolutions. This enables both qualitative and quantitative assessment in the absence of ground truth. We investigate two representative scenarios with sparse and ultra-sparse X-ray datasets and validate this approach using 4D-ONIX, a 4D deep-learning reconstruction method, on simulated water droplet collision experiments. The proposed approach provides a reference-free framework for performance estimation and support for better-informed experimental strategies across a wide range of ultrafast imaging applications.

articles.titulo: "Frozen" chromatin: insights on its structuring from cryo-EM tomography.
articles.revista: Chromosome research : an international journal on the molecular, supramolecular and evolutionary aspects of chromosome biology
articles.autores: Golyshev S, Kazakov E, Kireev I
articles.resumo_original: Chromatin is a DNA-protein polymer that ensures the safekeeping and realization of genetic information in eukaryotic cells. The genome of higher eukaryotes is packed into a relatively small nuclear volume and organized in a non-random yet non-deterministic manner, exhibiting a high degree of complexity and flexibility. Despite the dense packing of chromatin, the cell effectively controls transcription, replication, and DNA repair. Genomic approaches, direct visualization, and computer modeling have allowed to accumulate a large amount of data on the structure and behavior of chromatin in various functional states. However, many of these techniques rely on chemical cross-linking, membrane permeabilization, or altered ionic conditions, which may perturb native chromatin structure. This has led to contradictory views on chromatin organization in situ. Cryo-electron microscopy (Cryo-EM) ensures preservation of the cellular structures in a close to native hydrated state and provides high resolving power, thus becoming a tool of choice for studying organization of chromatin at the nucleosomal and supranucleosomal scales. This review summarizes how cryo-EM has advanced our understanding of chromatin organization and function, considers the limitations of the method, and discusses future directions and perspectives in the field.

articles.titulo: EMC chaperone activity is required for cotranslational calcium channel assembly.
articles.autores: Stanton M, Scheuing CE, Biswal M, Singal B, Agarwal M, Vargas GD, Gao A, Brademan DR, Hüttenhain R, Gifford CA, Pleiner T
articles.resumo_original: Nearly half of the ~5,000 human membrane proteins need to assemble into stoichiometric complexes as part of their biogenesis at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane. How ER-resident biogenesis factors coordinate membrane insertion, folding and assembly is not well understood. Here we demonstrate that the human ER membrane protein complex (EMC) insertase additionally acts as a chaperone to facilitate the assembly of heterotrimeric voltage-gated calcium channels (Cav). Using function-separating mutations and inhibitory nanobodies, we show that nascent Cav channels are degraded prematurely when EMC's chaperone function is selectively perturbed. Blocking EMC's chaperone function impaired Cav-dependent cardiomyocyte contraction. EMC engagement of the pore-forming Cav α-subunit occurred cotranslationally and required the Cav α-subunit's first transmembrane domain bundle to protrude from the nascent ribosome-multipass translocon complex. Our findings establish a chaperone function for the EMC and suggest that biogenesis of multibundle membrane proteins may require a highly orchestrated, cotranslational interplay among ER biogenesis factors.

articles.titulo: Cholesterol binding stabilizes the activated state of THIK-1 and promotes atherosclerosis.
articles.autores: Dai Z, Li Y, Hou Z, Duan G, Hu Z, Yang A, Wang Q, Wang W, Luo J, Zuo P, Yin Y, Yin Y
articles.resumo_original: Atherosclerosis, a chronic inflammatory disorder, remains a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality. While cholesterol is known to activate the NLRP3-IL-1β pathway and promote plaque formation, the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify the tandem pore domain halothane-inhibited potassium channel 1 (THIK-1) as a mediator of IL-1β release during atherosclerosis progression. Using high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), we determine the structure of THIK-1 in its apo form and in complex with the activator arachidonic acid, and the inhibitors halothane and C101248 as well as the structure of the disease-related THIK-1 R92S variant. Structural analyses reveal that cholesterol unexpectedly stabilizes the arachidonic acid-binding pocket within THIK-1. Complementary cellular assays confirm that cholesterol amplifies the arachidonic acid-induced inflammatory response in macrophages, which can be effectively suppressed by the THIK-1 inhibitors halothane and C101248. Moreover, treatment with C101248 markedly reduces atherosclerotic plaque development in Apoe-deficient mice fed a high-cholesterol diet. Collectively, these findings elucidate a cholesterol-dependent mechanism of THIK-1 regulation and highlight THIK-1 as a regulator of atherosclerosis.

articles.titulo: A multimeric pore complex in the poxvirus core revealed by integrative structural analysis.
articles.autores: Liu J, Schäfer S, Lehnung S, Baumann LM, Mühlberg L, Steiner C, Schreiber M, Linder M, Welsch S, Liu F, Bogdanow B, Krijnse Locker J, Turoňová B
articles.resumo_original: It has long been known that poxviruses transcribe more than a hundred early mRNAs within their viral core, yet how these transcripts exit the core remains unknown. Here, we combine cryo-electron tomography with deep-learning-based particle picking, subtomogram averaging, cross-linking mass spectrometry, and AlphaFold3 modeling to resolve the molecular architecture of a long-sought pore within the poxvirus core. The pore is formed by a heteromeric assembly of the viral proteins E8, E6, and L3, which together create a hollow hexameric tube spanning both the core wall and the surface-exposed palisade layer. Within the pore channel, we observe a rod-like density consistent with the viral RNA helicase I8, which may contribute to the release of the newly synthesized viral mRNAs from the core. We further observe a state of the pore lacking the outer and basal rings under transcription conditions. Together, our findings identify the structure and dynamics of a candidate mRNA-release pore within the surface layer of a double-stranded DNA virus and suggest that it may form part of the poxvirus transcription machinery.

articles.titulo: Revisit of the admitted control RND efflux pumps' inhibitor PAβN: use limitations, and structural revelation in complex with MexB.
articles.autores: Wehbi H, Olivier E, Cece Q, Mégret M, Sébastien M, Aissaoui N, Llanes C, Phan G, Broutin I
articles.resumo_original:
To bypass the health problem of antibiotic resistance in Gram-negative bacteria, a tempting approach is to use efflux pump inhibitors (EPI) to block the transporters before they expel antibiotics from the cell. One well-known EPI is the phenylalanine-arginine beta-naphthylamide (PAβN). Although it is described as toxic and therefore unsuitable for clinical use, it is highly effective and is commonly used as EPI reference compound in drug development. Nevertheless, the lack of toxicity on several cellular strains in our hands required us to revisit this known RND inhibitor, to redefine its limits.
The rational design of new EPIs requires the integration of complementary information on their microbiological activity, toxicity toward eukaryotic cells, and description of molecular interaction with their target at atomic resolution. These parameters should also be considered in comparison with those of an established reference compound such as PAβN. Accordingly, the effect of PAβN on Pseudomonas aeruginosa was evaluated by determining the minimum inhibitory concentrations of three β-lactam antibiotics in the presence or absence of PAβN and by defining concentrations that do not perturb the bacterial envelope. Its toxicity was assessed using four human cell lines and multiple cellular endpoints. Finally, the interaction of PAβN with the RND transporter MexB was characterized by cryo-electron microscopy and crystallography.
Microbiological analyses defined concentration ranges in which PAβN can be used to investigate efflux inhibition without causing detectable perturbation of the bacterial envelope. Across the four human cell models, PAβN displayed limited cytotoxicity, whereas β-naphthylamine was markedly more toxic. This points to the β-naphthylamide moiety as a potential contributor to PAβN toxicity, possibly resulting from metabolic proteolysis processing. Structural analyses revealed PAβN bound to MexB in the Tight conformation in both cryo-EM and crystal structures, but at distinct positions within the binding cavity. Comparison with the previously reported structure of PAβN bound to the artificially symmetric trimer of AcrB provides new insights into PAβN recognition and handling by RND pumps. Together, these microbiological, toxicological, and structural data refine the use of PAβN as a reference EPI and provide new perspectives on substrate transport by RND efflux pumps.

articles.titulo: Key factors for growth and phosphate uptake by Acinetobacter tjernbergiae.
articles.autores: Brück J, Täuber S, Ackermann L, Schittkowski H, Neubauer P, Junne S
articles.resumo_original: Phosphorus-containing fertilisers are essential for global food production but depend on finite phosphate rock reserves. Recovery of phosphorus from waste streams, such as those in wastewater treatment plants, will be required to follow future regulations. Certain Acinetobacter spp. can accumulate 24-30% (w w-1) of phosphate intracellularly, making them promising candidates for microbial phosphorus recovery. However, previous studies have reported insufficient biomass formation to enable rapid phosphate uptake. Therefore, this work investigated key factors of biomass generation and phosphate uptake of Acinetobacter tjernbergiae in an empirical study. Increasing iron concentration by 1 mg L-1 enhanced growth six-fold in shake flask cultivations. A maximum biomass concentration of 12 ± 0.7 g L-1 was achievable during 14 h of bioreactor cultivation. The maximum volumetric phosphate uptake rate (rS,P) reached 280.2 ± 40.8 mg (L h)-1, the highest value reported so far for Acinetobacter spp., while specific rates of up to 41.0 ± 1.1 mg (g h)-1 were achieved. It was further shown that A. tjernbergiae exhibits both polyphosphate accumulation and the overplus phenomenon. Moreover, phosphate uptake was strongly correlated with carbon uptake, while carbon absence resulted in phosphate release.

articles.titulo: Role of phoU in P. aeruginosa virulence and the emergence of compensatory mutations in the ΔphoU mutant.
articles.autores: Machado GT, Picinin NG, Ferraz D, de Almeida LG, Thomaz L, Wolf SG, Elbaum M, Spira B
articles.resumo_original: Bacteria respond to phosphate (Pi) availability by modulating the PHO regulon, which encodes proteins for Pi scavenging. The phoU gene is part of the pst operon, a high-affinity phosphate transport system that also represses PHO regulon expression under Pi excess. In the absence of phoU, Pi transport continues but repression fails, resulting in constitutive PHO gene transcription. In Pseudomonas aeruginosa and other Proteobacteria, phoU knockouts display pleiotropic effects, including stress and antibiotic sensitivity and polyphosphate (polyP) accumulation. Here, using cryo-STEM imaging and EDX analysis, we show that the ΔphoU mutant of P. aeruginosa accumulates large polyP granules containing over seven-fold more phosphorus than the wild type. Moreover, ΔphoU was markedly less virulent in vivo in the Galleria mellonella model. We further isolated two suppressor classes from ΔphoU: low-constitutive alkaline phosphatase (LCAP) and not-constitutive alkaline phosphatase (NCAP). LCAP mutants remain PHO-constitutive, less virulent than wild type, and accumulate polyP similarly to ΔphoU. In contrast, NCAP mutants are not PHO-constitutive, do not accumulate polyP, and retain wild-type virulence. We also tested swarming motility, pyocyanin, and pyoverdine production. Significant differences were limited to swarming, where ΔphoU was substantially less motile than the wild type, with LCAP showing partial recovery and NCAP full restoration.

articles.titulo: A Glial Interplay Regulates Junctional Architecture at the Blood-Brain Barrier of Drosophila.
articles.autores: Contreras EG, Naffin E, Collins-Ramírez M, Surina NV, Rothermel M, Salazar-Tirado J, Schirmeier S, Klämbt C
articles.resumo_original: Neurons require a tightly controlled ion and metabolite homeostasis, which is maintained by an effective blood-brain barrier (BBB). Since the integrity of the BBB is essential for brain function, its maintenance during development represents a significant challenge. The Drosophila BBB is formed by two glial layers. Subperineurial glia (SPG) establish pleated septate junctions (pSJs) to generate the primary diffusion barrier. Abutting the SPG lies the mitotically active perineurial glia (PG). Only a small number of PG cells are specified during embryogenesis. The FGF8-like signal Pyramus presented by the SPG subsequently triggers proliferation of the PG, which ultimately covers the entire nervous system. To investigate the role of PG in the development and physiology of the BBB, we genetically ablated them. In these animals, glucose influx into SPG is unchanged following acute glucose perfusion. However, adult PG-ablated flies show increased sensitivity to glucose-only diet, indicating that while baseline carbohydrate transport can be maintained in the absence of most PG, the system fails under metabolic stress. SPG morphology and pSJ organization are largely preserved during larval stages upon PG ablation. In contrast, in PG-ablated pupae, moody expression is impaired in SPG and pSJs progressively split, producing ectopic junctional strands. Together, these results reveal the necessity of PG for the maturation and function of SPG, as well as the mutual interdependence between the two BBB glial layers.

articles.titulo: The Fat-Body Secreted Neuropeptide CCHa2 Signals Insulin-Producing Cells in the Brain to Promote Sleep.
articles.autores: Biglari S, Gong S, Wang MC, Payne CA, Kauffman MR, DiAngelo JR, Keene A
articles.resumo_original: Sleep is a fundamental behavior regulated by diverse environmental and physiological cues. While the central mechanisms underlying sleep regulation have been investigated in detail, far less is known about how nutrient signals from the periphery are communicated to the brain to modulate sleep. Here, we perform a targeted RNAi screen of genes enriched in the fat body and regulated by feeding state to identify genes that function in the fat body to regulate sleep in Drosophila. This analysis found that fat body-specific knockdown of CCHa2 significantly reduced sleep duration and sleep depth in fed flies, phenocopying sleep in starved flies. CCHa2-deficient flies exhibited reduced glycogen stores and diminished feeding drive. Analysis of single-cell transcriptomic atlases confirms that the CCHa2 receptor (CCHa2-R) is selectively expressed in insulin-producing cells (IPCs) of the fly brain. We find that knockdown of CCHa2-R in IPCs recapitulates the sleep loss phenotype of CCHa2 mutants, supporting a role in adipose-brain signaling. Further screening of genes identified in single cell atlases as being enriched in IPCs led to the identification of numerous genes that function in IPCs to regulate sleep, including modulators of wnt and insulin signaling. Together, these findings identify a fat body-IPC axis that is a critical modulator of sleep duration and intensity.

articles.titulo: Light pollution causes death, sleep loss, and cognitive impairments through systemic reactive oxygen species accumulation in bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) gynes.
articles.autores: Shi M, Guo Y, Wang Y, Wang S, Li J, Li Z
articles.resumo_original: Light pollution affects about one quarter of the Earth's land surface and is rapidly growing in both extent and intensity with accelerated global urbanization. Artificial light at night (ALAN) constitutes the major source of light pollution and poses significant challenges to the health of many organisms, including pollinators. However, whether and how ALAN exposure affects bumblebees' physiology remain unexplored. Our study aims to preliminarily investigate the effects of ALAN exposure on bumblebees and hypothesizes that it may cause physiological damage to gynes. As we expected, ALAN exposure causes precocious death in gynes. Extended light exposure leads to sleep loss and dysfunctional cognitive performance in gynes. In addition, light pollution also disrupts the nutritional homeostasis in gynes. Transcriptomic analysis revealed altered expression of genes associated with sleep, cognition, and nutrient metabolism, suggesting that ALAN exposure may disrupt gut-brain communication in gynes. Furthermore, systemic accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) is detected in ALAN-exposed gynes due to down-regulation of genes in the glutathione metabolic pathway. Importantly, both oral supplementation with antioxidants and dark recovery effectively suppress excessive ROS production and reverse the detrimental effects after ALAN exposure to gynes. Our study provides evidence of the detrimental effects of light pollution on gynes for the first time and reveals the pivotal role of oxidative stress in mediating light-induced sleep loss, cognitive impairment, and nutrient homeostasis disruption of bumblebees. This further implicates light pollution as a potential contributor to bumblebees' decline.

articles.titulo: Class-wide sequence, structural, and docking-profile diversity of insect odorant receptors and structural specialization of Orco.
articles.autores: Zhang T, Yang X, Fu Y, Xue W, Zhang Y, Duan S, Yin Y, Guo Y, Gao C, Liu Y, Li G, Xu C, Lu H
articles.resumo_original: Insect olfaction is facilitated by a heterotetrameric odorant receptor-odorant receptor co-receptor (OR-Orco) complex. However, extensive sequence divergence and lineage-specific expansion have complicated large-scale comparisons of OR repertoires across insects. Here, we integrated sequence similarity, structural similarity, and molecular docking to analyze ORs from 115 insect species. OR repertoire size was associated with adult diet, larval diet, and habitat, but not with circadian rhythm. We developed a 'trunk-branch' network framework to classify ORs according to sequence and structural similarity and used large-scale molecular docking to derive comparative docking profiles. Despite marked differences in sequence- and structural-community composition, almost all sampled orders contained ORs assigned to all six docking-profile communities. Holometabolous insects showed higher OR sequence-community diversity than non-holometabolous insects, and docking-profile composition differed between extant lineages whose order-level origins predate or postdate the end-Permian mass extinction. Most notably, we identified a highly conserved extracellular β-sheet in Orco that restricts ligand access to the binding pocket and may contribute to its reduced capacity to bind natural odorants. The emergence of Orco represents a key evolutionary transition from homomeric receptors to heteromeric OR-Orco complexes, and our results suggest that this transition may have been accompanied by pronounced specialization of the extracellular domain and binding pocket. Together, these analyses provide a class-wide framework for comparing insect OR diversity and generate testable hypotheses for future experimental and evolutionary studies.

articles.titulo: The Role of Drosophila Toll Receptors in the Central Nervous System.
articles.autores: Ma Z, Xu J, Yu XL, Wang X, Gu Q, Meng H
articles.resumo_original: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are evolutionarily conserved pattern recognition receptors that play pivotal roles in innate immunity by detecting pathogen-associated molecular patterns. While initially characterized for their function in dorsoventral patterning and antifungal defense in Drosophila, the Toll family is now understood to have undergone a functional expansion in the nervous system. This review synthesizes the current understanding of the nine Drosophila Toll receptors (Toll-1 to Toll-9) and their roles in the central nervous system (CNS). We discuss how these receptors, particularly through non-canonical signaling pathways, function as neurotrophin receptors and cell surface recognition molecules. They mediate a wide range of cellular processes, from axon guidance to synaptic partner matching and the regulation of neuronal survival versus apoptosis through the competitive recruitment of adaptor proteins such as dMyD88 and Sarm. We further explore the involvement of Toll signaling in adult brain structural plasticity, sleep homeostasis, and behavioral responses to environmental stressors such as ethanol. Importantly, this article addresses the context-dependent duality of Toll signaling in neuropathology, dysregulation, and aberrant activation, which are closely related to neurodegeneration, lifespan determination, and infection responses. Through this timely summary of current research, this review highlights the molecular switches that govern Toll receptor functional states and their roles in neuro-immune interactions, with implications for understanding neurological diseases in vertebrates.

articles.titulo: Cry1Ac-transgenic Populus × xiaohei Disrupts Digestive Physiology and Energy Homeostasis to Impair 20E-Dependent Molting in Hyphantria cunea Larvae.
articles.revista: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
articles.autores: Zhao YC, Li XL, Zhang L, Wang YT, Gou RM, Zhao XY, Zang LS
articles.resumo_original: Plant-delivered Cry proteins effectively control lepidopteran pests, but how midgut injury develops into systemic metabolic and developmental dysfunction remains unclear. Here, fourth instar Hyphantria cunea larvae were fed wild-type (WT), pair-fed wild-type (PF-WT), or Cry1Ac-transgenic Populus × xiaohei leaves. Cry1Ac-transgenic leaf feeding impaired nutrient utilization, growth, survival, and development, disrupted the chitin-associated midgut interface, and reduced α-amylase and lipase activities. Metabolites altered relative to both controls were enriched in glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, pyruvate metabolism, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and starch and sucrose metabolism. These changes were accompanied by reduced glycolytic activity, ATP content, and adenylate energy charge, increased AMPKα phosphorylation, reduced S6K and 4E-BP phosphorylation, and altered 20E biosynthesis, signaling, and chitin synthesis. Exogenous 20E partially restored molting-related gene expression, epidermal chitin, molting success, and developmental timing, but not feeding or growth. These findings support a proposed digestive-metabolic-endocrine model associated with Cry1Ac-induced molting impairment.

articles.titulo: Chemosensory Protein 10 (CSP10) Is Involved in Resistance to Chlorantraniliprole in Spodoptera frugiperda.
articles.revista: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
articles.autores: Xu D, Guo Z, Xia G, Ling S, Zhang G, Tian X, Ma K
articles.resumo_original: Spodoptera frugiperda, an economically important agricultural pest, has developed high resistance to chlorantraniliprole, yet mechanisms beyond metabolic detoxification and target-site mutations remain unclear. Chemosensory proteins (CSPs) have emerged as novel contributors to insecticide resistance via direct sequestration. Here, the transcript abundance of 22 CSPs was evaluated in susceptible (SS) and chlorantraniliprole-resistant (CAP-RR) strains of S. frugiperda using transcriptomics and RT-qPCR. Results showed that CSP10 was notably upregulated in the CAP-RR strain and inducible by the insecticide exposure. RNAi-mediated silencing of CSP10 significantly increased larval susceptibility to chlorantraniliprole. Fluorescence binding assays confirmed strong affinity between CSP10 and chlorantraniliprole. Molecular docking and dynamics further revealed the binding interaction primarily via van der Waals forces. Site-directed mutagenesis coupled with computational alanine scanning revealed Phe6, Ile17, Tyr21, Val25, and Phe38 as critical residues for the interaction. Collectively, our findings establish CSP10 as a key mediator of chlorantraniliprole resistance, offering a promising target for resistance management strategies.

articles.titulo: A gut symbiotic bacterium enhances baculovirus resistance in Spodoptera frugiperda by maintaining peritrophic matrix integrity.
articles.autores: Guo L, Jin W, Kang Q, Tong Y, Shi H, Zhang J, Li X, Wang H, Qin Q, Meng Q, Zhang H
articles.resumo_original:
Spodoptera frugiperda is a major agricultural pest worldwide, whereas Spodoptera frugiperda multiple nucleopolyhedrovirus (SfMNPV) serves as an important microbial control agent against this pest. Resident gut bacteria are increasingly recognized as important modulators of insect-pathogen interactions; however, whether and how they influence SfMNPV infection in S. frugiperda remains unclear. We therefore investigated how gut bacteria modulate host resistance to SfMNPV.
Antibiotic-mediated depletion of gut bacteria increased larval susceptibility to SfMNPV. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed that gut bacterial depletion downregulated midgut genes associated with immune defense, digestive functions and peritrophic matrix (PM) maintenance. Among seven culturable midgut bacterial isolates, reinoculation with Glutamicibacter soli significantly enhanced larval resistance to SfMNPV. Pre-feeding with either the G. soli culture supernatant or cell lysis precipitate also increased larval resistance and partially reversed transcriptional changes caused by gut bacterial depletion before viral challenge, including the downregulation of peritrophin-1. RNAi-mediated silencing of peritrophin-1 disrupted PM structure, increased PM permeability, and enhanced larval susceptibility to SfMNPV. Consistently, G. soli reinoculation restored PM integrity impaired by gut bacterial depletion.
These findings identify maintenance of PM integrity as an important mechanism contributing to gut symbiotic bacterium-mediated resistance to SfMNPV. The study advances our understanding of how gut bacteria influence baculovirus infection in insect hosts and provides potential microbial and molecular targets for improving baculovirus-based pest management. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
